name: OSPO
quotableDefinition: An Open Source Program Office (OSPO) is the team inside an organization — a company, university, or government agency — responsible for how that organization uses, contributes to, and releases open source software.
body:
OSPOs grew out of industry practice in the 2000s and 2010s, as companies like Google and Microsoft found they needed one place responsible for open source policy, license compliance, and how staff engage with outside projects. Universities followed for the same reason: research software and research computing made the same coordination gap visible in academia.

The UC OSPO Network applies that model across the University of California system — not one central office, but a cross-campus network of OSPO-aligned staff sharing practice, education, and support, since not every campus runs this function the same way yet.

faq.question: Is an OSPO the same as a licensing or legal office?
faq.answer: No. Legal review is often one input, but an OSPO's scope is broader — developer support, contribution workflows, community engagement, and open source strategy, not just compliance sign-off.

faq.question: Does every UC campus have its own OSPO?
faq.answer: Not yet uniformly. The UC OSPO Network exists partly to support campuses building this function and to share practice between the ones that already have it.
